prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B035 to B029. In round 1 I called B029 the best-bounded and best-attributed case on the list and said I would support it; after reading all eight statements and the chair's questions I think my own first choice cannot be repaired within the rules, and B029 can be defended on its merits, not only on its support count. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping is a single, identifiable idea: it removes Doppler and recoil shifts and keeps a large number of atoms, which is what gives both low systematic uncertainty and high stability. Ye's group realised it at the 10^-18 level and showed many-body and relativistic effects inside the clock. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) reproduce and intercompare the performance, so the result is mature as a measurement. Every member who named laureates chose the same two names. For the chair's first question, I read the 2005 prize as covering the frequency comb as a readout and spectroscopy tool and the 2012 prize as covering the control of single trapped quantum systems. Neither covers trapping many neutral atoms in a lattice at a wavelength where the clock transition is not shifted. That is a different route to accuracy, and the citation should say so by naming magic-wavelength trapping and not just a precision number.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is a real reservation, and I do not treat it as settled by assertion. The lattice clock reads out through the comb and competes directly with Al+ ion clocks, so a sceptic can call it a continuation of an honoured line. Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley and the Yb lattice and Al+ groups reached comparable accuracy, and a record number is not an idea held by two people, which is why I want the citation tied to the lattice concept and its realisation. I am a theorist in condensed matter and not a metrologist, so on how much of the 10^-18 result belongs to the lattice concept and how much to laser stabilisation and cavity engineering I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would not let it carry the case, because the merit is the measured performance and the idea behind it. The cost of my change is that I give up what I still regard as the most fundamental new idea on the shortlist, B035.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce asked whether the committee can say why Katori and Ye, and not Lemonde, Ludlow or Lisdat, are credited, and whether the citation can rest on magic-wavelength trapping and many-atom lattice clocks without the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I think it can, provided the citation names the concept and its realisation and omits any record number or future redefinition. The idea is Katori's and the first demonstration of the accuracy regime at that level is Ye's. Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and the ion-clock groups reached comparable performance later or by other routes, and they are the reason I would not write 'the most accurate clock' into the wording. If a supporter can show that a third person made a decisive contribution to the concept and not to later accuracy records, I would listen. Without that, I do not see a principle that adds a name, and I would not change the pair to satisfy the length of the shortlist.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the Hall-Haensch comb is how the clock is read out and not how it is made accurate, so the 2005 overlap is smaller than the ballots suggest, and that waiting for the redefinition of the second is not a scientific criterion.
responses.response: Her distinction moves me, and it was the missing piece in my round-1 hesitation. The comb makes the clock countable and the lattice makes it accurate, so the new step is in the trapping and not in the readout. I agree that waiting for a metrological decision is not a scientific test. I would still keep the 2012 overlap on the record, because Al+ ion clocks are the direct competitors, and I would want the citation to avoid language that treats lattice and ion clocks as one achievement. On B031, where she lists it as her first alternative, I agree about the prediction preceding the experiment but not about timing, because the origin of the correlated states is not settled.

responses.point: Kroll asks to include new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second in the B029 citation, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, which the chair asks the committee to treat as either recusal or disclosure.
responses.response: I would keep the citation to the invention and the realisation and leave the tests of constants out of the wording. Nobody has yet used the clocks to find a violation, so the prospective physics should be context and not credit. On the disclosure, a research stay in a laboratory near Ye's environment, with no collaboration, supervision or shared funding, is a reason to record it and not a reason for recusal. The outcome does not depend on his view, because Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce reached B029 on their own, and I reached it after a different starting point. I would ask only that the minutes show his disclosure.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the Higgs discovery is the clearest concrete discovery on the shortlist and that the experimental side is overdue, and he proposes Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee as founders and long-time leaders of ATLAS and CMS.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance, the maturity or the claim that the experimental side deserves recognition. My difficulty remains the attribution, and your round-1 answer states the problem well: spokespersons at the time of discovery, detector pioneers and accelerator leaders have comparable claims. I put the same standard on my own B035, where Metzner's omission is an equivalent gap, and I withdrew it for that reason. I am willing to look again if you can show a decisive individual contribution to the discovery itself, and not only to the conception and construction of the detectors. At present the citation rewards leadership of two projects, and I cannot defend three names from that.

responses.point: Johansson, who is not an expert in the area of B035, pressed whether Metzner's omission is resolvable and whether it creates a larger fairness problem than the overlap questions on the clock.
responses.response: This is also the chair's question to me. I do not think it is resolvable within three names. Metzner and Vollhardt made the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar made the impurity mapping, and Mueller-Hartmann, Jarrell and Rozenberg did decisive early work. A citation that omits any of them is open to the same objection, and dropping Vollhardt to include Metzner would be worse. So I now say that B035 does not hold as drafted, and your point was fair. I do not think this tells against the science, which I still consider more fundamental than the clock, but the rules of the prize decide the configuration and not my ranking of ideas.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, but I cannot judge the metrology as well as Kroll or Lindroth.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat or the Yb and Al+ ion-clock groups hold a claim to the 10^-18 milestone that a two-name citation obscures.
Whether B035 could be made fair with a different naming rule, which I doubt, so I leave it as an alternative for a later year.
Whether the origin of the superconductivity and correlated states in B031 will be settled soon enough that it becomes the better choice than B029 in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: My own research uses DFT and DFT+DMFT, so I am a user and a potential beneficiary of B035, which I no longer propose; my preference now lies in a different part of physics. B031 is close to my field of electronic-structure theory. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which bears on any B004 discussion. My record shows no link to Katori, Ye or the optical clock community, so I see no recusal conflict for B029. I support recording Kroll's Hall-laboratory connection as a disclosure and not as a reason for recusal.
